abstract: Soybean (Glycine max), a versatile cash crop, is the largest global source of plant-based protein and second-largest source of vegetable oil. However, soybean cyst nematode (SCN; Heterodera glycines) is the most economically damaging pest of soybean worldwide, causing substantial yield losses annually. Currently, the effectiveness of widely deployed genetic resistance in soybean cultivars is increasingly challenged by evolving SCN populations; therefore, identifying new sources and mechanisms of SCN resistance is critical. Crop wild relatives, the ancestral or closely related wild species of domesticated crops, are rich sources of genetic diversity encompassing various beneficial traits, including pathogen resistance. In this study, we applied a comparative, multi-omics approach to examine the molecular mechanisms underlying SCN resistance in wild soybean (Glycine soja). We integrated transcriptomic, metabolomic, and proteomic data from two wild soybean genotypes representing contrasting responses to SCN (S54, resistant; S67, susceptible) at early- and late-stage infection. Our results reveal distinct constitutive molecular profiles and contrasting genotype-specific responses to SCN infection. The resistant genotype S54 exhibited a stronger early transcriptional response, particularly involving defense signaling and stress-responsive processes, whereas the susceptible genotype S67 showed a delayed response. Gene co-expression and integrative multi-omics analyses identified coordinated molecular networks associated with resistance, including defense-related genes and metabolic features. Together, these findings suggest that SCN resistance in wild soybean involves both pre-existing molecular differences and early activation of defense-associated responses. Our work identifies candidate genes, metabolites, and pathways for future functional testing. Ultimately, these findings provide an integrated multi-omics view of SCN resistance mechanisms in wild soybean, extending our understanding beyond commonly studied cultivar-based resistance and offering potential targets for soybean improvement.
